title: Not by eye, not by speech — by the mind made pure (3.1)
hook: the Mundaka lists the ways the self can't be grasped, and then names the one way it can: a mind gone clear
tomorrow: the rivers lose their names in the sea

segments.voice: Yesterday: truth alone prevails, and your line, the motto on the coins. Did handling money remind you to straighten one small crooked thing? Day four hundred nineteen.

Scoop up a glass of river water after a storm. It's brown, swirling, you can't see a thing through it. Now set it on the counter and leave it alone. You don't filter it. You don't stir it. You just let it be. An hour later, the mud has settled to the bottom, and you can see straight through to the other side. Nothing was added. Something just stopped moving. The Mundaka has been telling us about the self for two chapters. Now it tells us how it's seen, and first, how it isn't.
screen: `A GLASS OF MUDDY RIVER WATER.` → `LEAVE IT ALONE.` → `AN HOUR LATER, CLEAR.`

segments.voice: The verse starts with a list of no. Na chakshusha grihyate: it isn't grasped by the eye. Not by speech either. Not by the other senses. Not by austerity, and not by works. That's a surprising list, because two of those, austerity and ritual works, were honored earlier in this Upanishad: the rites were called true, and Brahman itself swelled by tapas. But they're not the hand that grasps it. Then comes the yes. Jnana-prasadena vishuddha-sattvah. By the clearness of knowledge, the one whose being is purified, meditating, sees it, the one without parts. Prasada means clearness, calm, settling, like water once the mud has sunk. It can also mean grace and favor, and the same word names the blessed food given out at temples. Here it's knowledge gone clear. And vishuddha-sattva is a being made thoroughly clean. The next verse says how. The self is subtle, and known by thought, by a mind in which the five breaths have entered, and the whole mind of creatures is woven through with the senses. When that mind is purified, the self shines out. So the senses, speech, discipline and ritual aren't thrown away. They're more like the stirring stick and the filter. Useful. But the seeing happens when the water stops moving. And the verse ends with meditating: in this picture, not one more technique to add, but a mind sitting still long enough to become clear.
screen: `NOT BY EYE, NOT BY SPEECH.` · `NOT BY AUSTERITY OR WORKS.` · `BY THE CLEARNESS OF KNOWLEDGE.` · `A PURIFIED MIND, AND THE SELF SHINES.` · then, large: `JNANA-PRASADA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes as the glass of water. Sit still, and let whatever is stirred up in you be stirred up: today's conversations, a worry, a song stuck in your head. Don't try to filter it. Don't stir. Just stop adding motion. See whether, with each breath, some of it sinks a little lower. You don't have to make the water clear. You only have to leave it alone, and look. The bell holds the time.
Not by eye. In the Mundaka, the self isn't grasped by eye, speech, austerity or works, but by the clearness of knowledge, in a mind made pure.
Your line: purified. Today, when your mind gets muddy, stop stirring for one minute and let something settle before you decide anything. Day four hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: In Vedanta teaching, practices like japa, meditation, fasting and worship are often described as ways of purifying the mind (chitta-shuddhi), so that knowledge can arise, rather than as ends in themselves.

match.prompt: how the self is seen — tap the pairs.

myth: the Mundaka says the self is grasped by austerity
not by austerity, not by works: by the clearness of knowledge.
prasada can mean clearness and also grace
temple food called prasad shares the word.
the next verse says a purified mind lets the self shine out
when the mind is purified, the self shines forth.

fork.setup: the self isn't grasped by the eye, by speech, by austerity or by works. what does the Mundaka name instead?
options: the clearness of knowledge, in a mind made pure.
fork.reveal: jnana-prasadena vishuddha-sattvah: by the clearness of knowledge, one whose being is purified, meditating, sees the partless.

original.note: Sanskrit jñāna-prasāda: jñāna, knowledge, + prasāda, clearness, serenity. Mundaka 3.1.8.

trapdoor: what you thought: you find God by trying harder.
what it means: the self isn't grasped by senses, speech, austerity or works, but seen when the mind becomes clear.
what a scholar hears: na cakṣuṣā gṛhyate nāpi vācā nānyair devais tapasā karmaṇā vā; jñānaprasādena viśuddhasattvas tatas tu taṃ paśyate niṣkalaṃ dhyāyamānaḥ (3.1.8).

sources.ref: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.9 (known by thought; when the mind is purified, the self shines)

notes: 3.1.8–9 paraphrased; 'by a mind in which the five breaths have entered' renders yasmin pranah pancadha samvivesha. Confirm.
The muddy-water illustration is the script's own, not the text's.
prasada/prasad link is lexical (same word), stated carefully; confirm.
Chitta-shuddhi in howItsDone is a later Vedanta term; confirm framing.
